code.originalText: Periodic adult preventive visit after ovarian cancer treatment

text.paragraph: Periodic adult preventive visit, four weeks into olaparib. [S]

Ms. Radner, now 40, comes for her yearly preventive visit four weeks after starting olaparib maintenance. She finished six cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel seven weeks ago; the end-of-treatment CT showed no evidence of disease and her CA-125 was 9. On olaparib she has mild nausea in the first hour after the morning dose, which settles if she takes it with food, and she tires in the late afternoon. She has no breathlessness, cough, fever, or bruising. The tingling in her toes is fading. Hot flashes wake her two or three nights a week; she has chosen to wait on hormone therapy for now. She goes to a support group at a cancer support community every other week and is writing again. Her PHQ-9 today is 2. [S]

Persistent bloating with tightness of her clothes, feeling full after a few bites, a dull lower abdominal and pelvic ache, and passing urine more often, on most days for about four weeks, in a woman of 39: the ovarian cancer symptom index is positive. Examination: a distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a firm, fixed, irregular mass in the right adnexa. Suspected ovarian cancer; transvaginal ultrasound, CT, CA-125 and gynecologic oncology review booked within the week
S — Synthetic presenting problem linked to her documented abdominal symptoms; superseded by the diagnosis at the gynecologic oncology consultation.

High-grade serous carcinoma of both ovaries (Mullerian origin), diagnosed by image-guided omental core biopsy (PAX8 and WT1 positive, p53 aberrant), with bilateral adnexal masses, ascites, omental and diaphragmatic disease on CT: clinical FIGO stage IIIC; synthetic modern detail linked to her documented ovarian cancer
S — Synthetic histology and stage; the documented diagnosis was stage IV ovarian cancer (D).
Peritoneal and omental metastases of the ovarian cancer, with ascites
S — Synthetic extent of disease on CT and biopsy.
Family history of ovarian cancer in three relatives (her grandmother, an aunt, and a cousin) in a woman of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry; no genetic testing in the family is known
S — Synthetic coding of her documented family history; the basis for genetic counseling.

Acute viral upper respiratory infection on day 8 of the second chemotherapy cycle: two days of sore throat, runny nose and a dry cough, without fever; rapid influenza and COVID-19 tests negative; resolved
S — Synthetic acute infection; not a historical claim.
Symptomatic surgical menopause after bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy at 39: hot flashes and night sweats
S — Synthetic consequence of the synthetic operation.
Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy from paclitaxel: tingling in the toes and fingertips, grade 1 (sensory only, no effect on daily activities)
S — Synthetic common effect of paclitaxel.

Periodic adult preventive visit completed. Health risk assessment reviewed and the prevention plan updated for a woman of 40 after ovarian cancer treatment. Total cholesterol 186, HDL 58, LDL 108 mg/dL; ten-year cardiovascular risk under 2 percent, so no statin. Mammography is due now that she is 40. Cervical screening is no longer needed because the cervix was removed for a cancer that was not cervical. Vaccines for an adult after chemotherapy are given today, with no live vaccine. [S]
Influenza, COVID-19, PCV20 and the first recombinant zoster dose given today; the second zoster dose in two to six months.
Screening mammogram ordered.
Baseline bone density scan ordered after surgical menopause.
Next preventive visit in one year.

High-grade serous ovarian cancer, stage IIIC, no evidence of disease, on olaparib maintenance (C56.3). Four weeks of olaparib, well tolerated. Monthly blood count today: hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, a mild fall from 11.2 at the start, with white cells 4.2, neutrophils 2.4 and platelets 182; no dose change is needed. No breathlessness or new cough to suggest pneumonitis. [S]
Continue olaparib 300 mg twice daily with food.
Blood count again in four weeks.
Gynecologic oncology review with CA-125 three months after the end of chemotherapy.

Symptomatic surgical menopause (E89.41). Hot flashes two or three nights a week and vaginal dryness. Hormone therapy was discussed at the end of chemotherapy and is not ruled out by her cancer type; she prefers to wait. [S]
Vaginal moisturizer; layered bedding and a fan.
Revisit hormone therapy or a non-hormonal medicine at the next visit if sleep worsens.
Bone density scan as above.

Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (G62.0). Mild and fading seven weeks after the last paclitaxel; no effect on balance. [S]
Foot checks and well-fitting shoes; report any fall.

Follow-up: Mammogram and bone density scan within the month. Blood count in four weeks. Gynecologic oncology review in about five weeks. Second zoster dose in two to six months. Next preventive visit in one year. [S]

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 20 minutes, with her consent. She named a health care agent, recorded in the confidential part of the chart and not named here. She said that she wants to be told the truth about her illness plainly and in person, that she would want treatment aimed at living longer as long as she can still enjoy her days and be herself, and that if that were no longer possible she would want comfort and to be awake enough to know the people around her. She completed a health care proxy form and will think about a written living will. To be revisited at each change in her health and at least yearly. [S]
